b: At rest, ion gradients and membrane permeability maintain the resting membrane potential.
Depolarisation usually occurs when voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium enters.
Repolarisation mainly occurs as potassium leaves through voltage-gated potassium channels.

In myelinated axons, saltatory conduction allows impulses to be regenerated at the nodes of Ranvier, increasing conduction speed.

Absolute refractory period: The time during which no amount of stimulus, no matter how strong, can elicit another action potential (due to inactivated sodium channels).

qs.q: A neurophysiologist records from a sensory neuron during sustained mechanical indentation of the skin. The receptor shows a rapid initial burst of action potentials followed by complete cessation of firing despite maintained pressure. How is this receptor classified?
qs.e: Rapidly adapting or phasic receptors respond strongly to the onset of a stimulus and then quickly adapt, ceasing activity during sustained pressure.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Neurophysiology I Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A neuroscientist measures the frequency of action potentials in a cutaneous mechanoreceptor while varying indentation force. What fundamental sensory coding principle relates stimulus intensity to action potential firing frequency?
o: Temporal dispersion of impulse train frequencies
Recruitment of neighboring units in population
Rate modulation of action potential firing frequency
qs.e: Sensory receptors encode stimulus intensity by altering the firing frequency of action potentials through rate coding.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Neurophysiology I Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: An experimental drug is applied to a nerve axon, preventing the repolarization phase of the action potential. Which specific ion channel or transporter was most likely blocked?
qs.e: Repolarization depends on the efflux of potassium ions through activated voltage-gated potassium channels following depolarization.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Physiology Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: During the absolute refractory period of a neuronal action potential, a second suprathreshold stimulus fails to elicit a response. What is the structural basis for this?
o: Sodium channels are in an inactivated state.
Potassium channels are fully closed down.
ATP stores are completely exhausted out.
qs.e: Voltage-gated sodium channels adopt an inactivated conformation that cannot reopen until membrane hyperpolarization resets them.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Physiology Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: What is the primary physiological significance of the plateau phase in a ventricular myocardial action potential?
o: To allow complete repolarization of sodium
To facilitate rapid passive filling of ventricles
To prevent tetanic contractions by extending
To halt all calcium movement into the cytosol
qs.e: The long plateau phase maintains a prolonged refractory period, ensuring the heart muscle cannot undergo tetanic contraction.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Physiology Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: Which mechanism prevents continuous firing of an action potential when a sustained depolarizing stimulus is applied to an unmyelinated axon?
qs.e: Sustained depolarization leads to the time-dependent inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels, terminating further action potentials.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Physiology Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: During an action potential in a large myelinated axon, which specific ionic conductance peaks earliest and triggers the rapid upstroke phase?
qs.e: The rapid upstroke of an action potential is driven by the early, rapid activation of voltage-gated sodium channels.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Physiology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A neuroscientist applies tetraethylammonium (TEA) to a giant axon and stimulates it. Which phase of the action potential is selectively impaired by this procedure?
o: Initial depolarization threshold is raised significantly
Repolarization phase is severely slowed or blocked
Absolute refractory period is shortened drastically
Resting potential shifts to positive millivolts
qs.e: TEA is a classic blocker of voltage-gated potassium channels, delaying membrane repolarization after an action potential.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Physiology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: An action potential is a rapid, all‑or‑nothing change in membrane potential that propagates along excitable cells, enabling nerve impulses and muscle contraction. It is driven by voltage‑gated ion channels and is essential for coordinated cardiac and nervous function.

sections.p: An action potential is a brief, large depolarization of a cell membrane that travels along the cell, allowing rapid communication between cells.
b: All‑or‑nothing: either a full spike or none

sections.p: Depolarization opens voltage‑gated Na⁺ channels, causing Na⁺ influx. Repolarization follows with K⁺ efflux through voltage‑gated K⁺ channels. In cardiac cells, Ca²⁺ influx sustains the plateau.

t.b: Shows characteristic phases of cardiac AP; abnormal patterns suggest channelopathies.

sections.p: The refractory period, modulated by ion channel kinetics, prevents back‑propagation and ensures unidirectional conduction. Autonomic tone adjusts channel activity.

t.b: Detects conduction delays or blocks; abnormal intervals indicate channel dysfunction.

sections.p: Mutations in ion channel genes, electrolyte imbalances, or drug effects can alter AP shape, leading to arrhythmias or muscle weakness.

t.b: Prolonged QT predicts torsades de pointes risk.
Low K⁺ shortens AP, causing arrhythmias; high K⁺ prolongs AP.

sections.p: AP abnormalities manifest as arrhythmias, syncope, or sudden death. Recognizing patterns guides drug choice and urgent interventions.

t.b: Identifies paroxysmal arrhythmias; informs antiarrhythmic selection.
Elevated LDH may indicate myocardial injury affecting AP.

sections.p: Remember the all‑or‑nothing principle and the distinct phases of cardiac AP. Know how drugs like amiodarone prolong AP by blocking K⁺ channels.

t.b: Blocks K⁺ channels, prolongs repolarization, increases refractory period.

faq.q: What causes a prolonged QT interval?
faq.a: Electrolyte disturbances, certain drugs, congenital channelopathies, or structural heart disease.

faq.q: Why does hypokalemia lead to arrhythmias?
faq.a: Low K⁺ shortens repolarization, increasing excitability and risk of early afterdepolarizations.

faq.q: How does amiodarone affect the action potential?
faq.a: It blocks K⁺ channels, prolonging phase 3, thereby increasing refractory period and reducing arrhythmia recurrence.
